articles.title: Instituto identifica parasita em água que abastece Itapeva | G1
articles.standfirst: Secretaria Estadual da Saúde enviou 40 mil frascos de hipoclorito de sódio como desinfecção à população. Análise apontou organismos que aparecem na água com coliformes fecais contaminados.
articles.summary: Uma análise feita pelo Instituto Adolfo Lutz apontou um parasita na água que estava abastecendo a população em Itapeva (SP). A cidade registrou 2,6 mil casos de gastroenterite.
articles.body:
Uma análise feita pelo Instituto Adolfo Lutz apontou um parasita na água que estava abastecendo a população em Itapeva (SP). A cidade registrou 2,6 mil casos de gastroenterite em apenas 20 dias.

O resultado foi divulgado pelo instituto da capital paulista por meio de nota, encaminhada à TV TEM nesta quarta-feira (28). O documento aponta que foi encontrado na água o protozoário Cryptosporidium spp.

Já na análise clínica dos pacientes, além do protozoário Cryptosporidium spp. foi encontrada a bactéria Escherichia coli enteroagregativa, transmitidos na água contaminada com coliformes fecais.

🔎 O protozoário Cryptosporidium spp. afeta as células do intestino delgado e pode ser transmitido pela ingestão de água ou alimentos contaminados com fezes de humanos ou animais infectados. Ele causa diarréia intensa, cólicas, náuseas, vômitos e febre.

🔎 Já a Escherichia coli enteroagregativa adere às células da mucosa intestinal e secreta toxinas que danificam o intestino. A transmissão ocorre da mesma forma e causa diarréias líquidas, mal-estar e febre baixa, que podem durar mais de duas semanas e causar danos na absorção de nutrientes.

Devido às anomalias, a Secretaria Estadual de Saúde de São Paulo (SES-SP) fez uma reunião com a Companhia de Saneamento Básico do Estado de São Paulo (Sabesp), com o intuito de adotar as medidas necessárias para a normalização da água fornecida na cidade.

Em nota, a Sabesp informou que acesso, nesta quarta-feira, aos resultados divulgados pela Secretaria Estadual da Saúde sobre a identificação de microrganismos em duas amostras de água coletadas em 19 de outubro em uma praça pública de Itapeva.

A companhia afirma que análises de 227 amostras de água coletadas pela Companhia no município entre 01 e 27 de outubro indicaram conformidade com os padrões de potabilidade estabelecidos pela legislação vigente.

Como medida, a companhia disse que fará análises de amostras adicionais e renovação da água por meio de descargas de rede para reforçar a segurança e a qualidade da água e dar tranquilidade à população.

A TV TEM entrou em contato com a Prefeitura de Itapeva para solicitar esclarecimentos, mas não obteve retorno até a publicação desta reportagem.

Santa Casa de Itapeva (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

A Secretaria Estadual de Saúde de São Paulo (SES-SP) enviou 40 mil frascos de hipoclorito de sódio à população, após outras análises apontarem alterações na qualidade da água encanada da cidade.

🔎 O hipoclorito de sódio é um desinfetante químico, amplamente utilizado para desinfecção e saneamento. Ele elimina bactérias, vírus e parasitas, tornando a água segura para beber.

O município registrou, em cerca de 20 dias, 2,6 mil casos de virose na saúde pública . Os resultados apontaram alterações de cloração, cor e turbidez entre 22 de setembro e 7 de outubro, período em que os atendimentos médicos foram registrados.

Como orientação da Secretaria, a população deve consumir alimentos bem cozidos, higienizar corretamente as mãos antes de preparar alimentos e usar hipoclorito de sódio a 2,5%, para desinfecção da água.

Apesar das alterações, a Sabesp afirmou, também via nota, que não identificou anomalias na água encanada em Itapeva.

A apuração da administração municipal começou após 700 pessoas apresentarem sintomas semelhantes em apenas quatro dias. Entre os principais relatos estão vômito e diarreia.

O aumento da procura também foi percebido em uma farmácia da cidade, que precisou reforçar o estoque de medicamentos usados no tratamento desses sintomas.

Câmara Municipal de Itapeva (SP) — Foto: Reprodução

A Câmara Municipal de Itapeva abriu, na segunda-feira (26), uma Comissão Especial de Inquérito (CEI) para investigar a qualidade da água distribuída pela Sabesp.

O grupo que forma a comissão terá 90 dias para investigar a companhia pela qualidade da água oferecida à população. O requerimento de abertura da CEI foi assinado por 11 parlamentares, com cinco compondo a mesa. Veja os integrantes abaixo:

A investigação começará no dia 4 de novembro, com previsão de término entre o fim de fevereiro e o início de março de 2027, devido ao recesso legislativo em janeiro.

Segundo a Câmara, a CEI servirá para entender se houve falha no tratamento e no abastecimento de água, além de entender como isso está relacionado ao surto de gastroenterite.

Saiba quais são os sintomas de gastroenterite — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

A gastroenterite é uma inflamação do estômago e do intestino e pode provocar sintomas como diarreia, vômito, náuseas, dores abdominais e febre.

Conforme a Secretaria de Saúde de Itapeva, na maioria dos casos, a recuperação pode ocorrer em casa, com alguns cuidados. A principal recomendação é manter a hidratação, consumindo água, soro de reidratação e outros líquidos ao longo do dia para repor a quantidade perdida pelo organismo.

A alimentação também deve ser mantida, dando preferência a alimentos leves e de fácil digestão, como sopas, frutas e torradas. O repouso é indicado enquanto persistirem os sintomas.

Outro cuidado importante é a higiene das mãos, principalmente após ir ao banheiro e antes de preparar ou consumir alimentos. A medida ajuda a reduzir o risco de transmissão da doença para outras pessoas da casa.

A Secretaria de Saúde também orienta que medicamentos sejam utilizados somente com indicação médica.

articles.title: 'Shameful decision': Meloni fumes after court frees researcher accused of helping organise violent Milan protests
articles.summary: An Italian judge’s decision to release a university researcher accused of helping organise violent protests in Milan earlier this month drew an angry
articles.body: An Italian judge’s decision to release a university researcher accused of helping organise violent protests in Milan earlier this month drew an angry response from Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who denounced the ruling as “shameful."Meloni condemned the ruling in a social media video, calling it “an unbearable humiliation” of the work of police and investigators. She questioned how a state could protect law-abiding citizens in the face of such judicial decisions."I think this is an unbearable humiliation of the work of the police and investigators. I really don't know how a normal state can defend decent people in the face of these decisions by certain sections of the judiciary," she said in the video.Meloni’s reaction came after a Milan judge ordered the release of Youseef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian freelance journalist of Moroccan origin and a graduate in geopolitics, citing what she described as a “deeply flawed” police investigation.“There are no serious grounds for believing that (Siher) committed the offences with which he has been charged, nor is there a risk of flight,” judge Tiziana Landoni wrote in her ruling.Siher was detained by Milan prosecutors on October 24 on charges of incitement to commit crimes, aggravated by alleged terrorist motives. He has consistently denied any wrongdoing.Police identified him as the administrator of the Telegram group “October 17 Movement”, which was created following the violent protests in Milan.According to the detention order, he posted what investigators described as “subversive content” and messages urging protesters to gather on October 24 to commit offences against public order.However, judge Landoni noted that the comments in question had been posted by other group members, not Siher. “Siher was not found to have encouraged or in any way supported the violent actions advocated by those users,” she wrote.The case has drawn attention because prosecutors invoked a new offence introduced under a security decree enacted by Meloni’s government this month as part of its latest law-and-order crackdown.The offence carries prison terms of four to 12 years for organisers of groups that endanger public safety or cause damage while participating in public demonstrations.Siher’s arrest has raised concerns among legal observers and members of the Italian Bar Association.Critics have also questioned the extensive media coverage of the case, with some Italian newspapers portraying him as guilty and publishing detailed accounts of his life and family.(With Reuters inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Battle scars': Massive stitches on Captain Smit Machchhar head draw attention as UAE honours hero Indian pilot
articles.summary: A massive line of stitches running across the back of Captain Smit Machchhar’s head has brought the severity of the Indian pilot’s injuries into focus as
articles.body: A massive line of stitches running across the back of Captain Smit Machchhar’s head has brought the severity of the Indian pilot’s injuries into focus as he received a prestigious UAE honour for his role in thwarting the mid-air cockpit attack.Far-right UK leader Tommy Robinson shared a photograph of the scar on social media, praising Machchhar for his bravery. “Not all heroes wear capes. Some wear battle scars. Hero Indian Captain Smit Machchhar. The world salutes you,” Robinson wrote.The Indian captain and his fellow flydubai crew members were conferred the First Class Order of Zayed II by UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in recognition of their efforts to protect passengers during the September 30 incident aboard flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv.The medals were presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum at a presidential reception. The UAE leadership praised the crew for their courage, professionalism and commitment to passenger safety.Machchhar was seriously injured when his co-pilot allegedly attacked him with a crash axe and stabbed him inside the cockpit. The aircraft, carrying more than 170 people, reportedly plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the incident.Despite being covered in blood and severely wounded, Machchhar managed to release the cockpit door lock, allowing passengers and crew members to overpower the co-pilot. Two other flydubai pilots who were travelling on board then took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.The motive behind the alleged attack remains unclear. The co-pilot, identified by Israeli officials as an Omani national, was taken into custody.Machchhar was initially treated at a hospital in Tabuk before being transferred to Abu Dhabi for further treatment. Sheikh Hamdan had earlier visited him in hospital and praised his courage in helping avert a potential tragedy.The First Class Order of Zayed II is a high-level UAE civil decoration awarded in recognition of distinguished service and exceptional contributions. articles.title: 72 hours, 3 countries, 1 private jet: Flavio Bolsonaro’s wild escape to US
articles.summary: From refusing to concede defeat to crossing into Argentina under cover of a private flight plan and travelling through Ecuador before landing in Miami,
articles.body: From refusing to concede defeat to crossing into Argentina under cover of a private flight plan and travelling through Ecuador before landing in Miami, Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s journey to the United States unfolded over a frantic 72 hours. The 45-year-old arrived in Florida on Wednesday with his wife and two daughters, days after losing the presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and amid mounting uncertainty over his whereabouts.The journey came as Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports in connection with investigations into alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing. US officials, meanwhile, confirmed that Washington would issue visas to him and his family, with President Donald Trump saying he would have approved their entry.Here is how Bolsonaro’s journey unfolded, from his election defeat on Sunday to his arrival in Miami on Wednesday. Sunday: Election defeat and refusal to concedeBolsonaro lost the presidential runoff to Lula, securing around 48% of the vote against his rival’s 52%. Despite entering the second round after leading the first-round vote, he failed to secure the majority required to win the presidency.He refused to concede defeat and threatened to seek the annulment of the result, questioning a decision to extend voting hours at some polling stations. His challenge came even as several world leaders recognised Lula’s victory.Monday: Supreme Court orders passports surrenderedBolsonaro said in a social media video that federal police had served him with an order to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports. The notice was delivered outside the home where his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election.Flavio Bolsonaro said he would comply with the order and rejected speculation that he planned to flee Brazil. However, the deadline to surrender the documents was set for noon on Tuesday, adding urgency to the unfolding situation. Tuesday: Where is Flavio Bolsonaro?As the deadline passed, reports about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts began to conflict. Argentine news outlet Infobae reported that he had left Brazil for Argentina and was preparing to travel to the US by private jet.Argentine migration authorities initially said they had no record of him entering the country. Meanwhile, CNN Brasil and other media outlets reported that the senator had travelled to the US, with sources cited by Reuters also indicating that he was heading there.A senior US State Department official subsequently confirmed that Bolsonaro and his family would be issued visas and allowed to enter the country. Trump also questioned Brazil’s election, describing it as “very strange” and saying he thought it was “terrible”.Lula criticised Bolsonaro’s departure, describing it as “shameful”. Wednesday: Argentina, Ecuador and finally MiamiThe journey became clearer after Argentine migration authorities said Bolsonaro, his wife, Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and their daughters, Carolina and Luiza, entered Argentina at around 10.50pm local time on Tuesday. They crossed the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, linking Brazil with Argentina’s Misiones province.According to the authorities, the family then boarded a private charter operated by Baires Fly SA, whose filed flight plan listed Guayaquil, Ecuador, as the destination.Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft arriving in Guayaquil early on Wednesday before departing for Miami’s Opa-locka Executive Airport. The plane landed in Florida at around 10.31am Brasilia time, with Reuters TV images showing Bolsonaro disembarking alongside his wife and daughters.The route through Argentina and Ecuador resolved much of the confusion over his whereabouts, although it also raised questions about his decision to leave Brazil after the election and amid the passport order. Why did Bolsonaro leave Brazil?Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court in two cases involving alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. He has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged in the cases.His eight-year Senate term expires on January 31, 2027, after which he will lose the special jurisdiction that allows cases involving him to be heard by the Supreme Court.His departure also carries political implications beyond Brazil. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, lives in Texas and had publicly urged him to leave the country if he lost the election. Trump has expressed support for allowing the family into the US, while Argentina’s President Javier Milei had campaigned for Flavio Bolsonaro during the Brazilian election.For a candidate who had insisted he would remain in Brazil to lead the opposition, the journey from election defeat to Miami marked a dramatic turn in less than three days.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Quint Pottinger, the eighth-generation Kentucky farmer who uses autonomous tractors to save his 245-year-old family farm after three years of drought cut yields to 100-130 bushels per acre
articles.summary: After three years of drought, rising expenses and difficult conversations with his banker, eighth-generation Kentucky farmer Quint Pottinger was running
articles.body: After three years of drought, rising expenses and difficult conversations with his banker, eighth-generation Kentucky farmer Quint Pottinger was running out of ways to save his family’s 245-year-old farm. With costs already cut across seeds, fertilisers, labour and equipment, he needed a different solution. His answer came from an unexpected place: autonomous tractors.According to Farm Journal, Pottinger discovered Sabanto, a company developing technology to convert conventional tractors into autonomous machines, after his lender suggested further equipment savings could improve the farm’s cash flow. What began as an experiment has since changed how the family approaches planting and fieldwork.Three years of drought left the family farm strugglingPottinger’s family has farmed the same land in Kentucky for 245 years. However, three consecutive years of dry weather in July resulted in disappointing corn yields and mounting financial pressure.“For the last three years, we've had bad dry weather in July and we've been making 100 to 130. So, it's been hard to pay the bills,” Pottinger told Farm Journal.The farm typically expected yields of around 150 to 170 bushels per acre, making the decline particularly difficult.Pottinger recalled the anxiety of hearing from his lender during those years.“Well, you knew you were going to get a call from the banker. And you didn't know what his mood was going to be. And depending on how his mood was going to be would set your mood for the week,” he said.The family cut spending wherever possible, including on seeds, fertilisers, employees and equipment.“We cut everything. We even cut our equipment,” Pottinger said.But there was only so much they could reduce without affecting operations. As he explained, “If the rain doesn't show up, it doesn't matter what you put in the ground, it's not going to grow.”A conversation with his banker led him to autonomous farmingThe turning point came when Pottinger’s lender suggested finding further equipment savings. Unsure where else to cut costs, he began searching online.“So I just Googled autonomy, and a company called Sabanto popped up on Google,” he recalled.Sabanto was developing a system to convert conventional tractors into autonomous machines. Although its technology had not been fully developed for row-crop farming, Pottinger decided to test it.“They hadn't really developed anything for row cropping, but they wanted to, but nothing ready yet. And I thought, well, send the demo out. Let's just see,” he said.The demonstration convinced his father, Remy Pottinger, that the technology had potential.“Well, they came and demonstrated it last year. And when it got through, I told Quint, ‘How soon can you get it in here?’” his father recalled.Meet Geneva, the autonomous tractor controlled by a phoneThe family named its autonomous tractor Geneva, after Pottinger’s grandmother. Rather than being a purpose-built driverless robot, it is a conventional tractor fitted with technology that allows it to operate autonomously.“It's just a regular tractor that we can control with a cell phone,” Pottinger said.He can assign tasks and monitor the tractor remotely. According to him, setting up a mission takes around five minutes, allowing the family to plan many operations in advance.The tractor has already helped plant hundreds of acres. Using an upgraded John Deere 750 drill, the family planted 500 acres of rye, wheat and barley, along with another 300 acres of cover crops.“We're the first ones to do it and deploy it at this scale in the world,” Pottinger said, describing the family's experience with autonomous row-crop planting.How planting works without sitting in the tractor cabAutonomous technology has changed Pottinger’s daily routine, but human supervision remains essential.During planting season, he wakes up around 5.30 am, activates the tractor’s computer remotely and checks its cameras before starting the machine. Farm workers handle refuelling, replenishing seeds and maintenance, while Pottinger monitors its progress.“She plants for two hours. Mike comes in wherever field she's at. He'll stop her, put fuel in her, fill her up with seed, and do a full maintenance check on the drill on the tractor,” he explained.The tractor can then resume work remotely and continue into the evening.The system also proved useful during a wet planting season, when around 300 acres had to be replanted three times. Pottinger was able to manage one of the replanting operations remotely while travelling in Germany.However, Geneva still has limitations. The tractor cannot reverse independently, requiring careful planning of field layouts and turning points.“It cannot back up,” Pottinger said.Labour savings offer hope for the futureFor Pottinger, the main motivation behind adopting autonomous technology was making farming financially sustainable. He believes the approach could also help other growers reduce costs and use equipment for multiple tasks, including mowing, spraying and hay production.“Maybe not for everyone, maybe not now, but definitely has applications across a wide swath of growers that may use it,” he said.The family has not yet used Geneva for harvesting, although Pottinger has considered how autonomous tractors could eventually support combine harvesters by transporting grain carts.From working behind mules to operating self-driving tractorsFor a family that has farmed the same land for 245 years, adopting autonomous technology marks another chapter in its history of agricultural change.Pottinger recalled working with his grandfather as a child, cutting grass and hay behind two mules. Today, the family is using technology that allows a conventional tractor to complete assigned tasks with limited direct intervention.“My family's been here for 245 years. We've seen a lot of change, and I think that that's just bred into us,” he said.He added that the family continues to look for ways to evolve while serving its community.“We're always looking for how do we evolve to make sure we're serving our community, and that's what the farm is supposed to be,” he explained.After years of financial uncertainty, Pottinger says the farm no longer feels as though it is constantly fighting for survival. Asked whether he was still operating in survival mode, he replied, “I don't.”And when asked whether he was enjoying farming again, his answer was simple: “I'm having fun again.”You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, Madonna’s charity opened a children’s surgery centre in Malawi; by 2025, it reported life-saving operations for over 2,000 children a year, with care provided at a free public facility
articles.summary: A children’s hospital unit set up by pop star Madonna’s charity in Malawi now carries out more than 2,000 life-saving operations every year.
articles.body: A children’s hospital unit set up by pop star Madonna’s charity in Malawi now carries out more than 2,000 life-saving operations every year. It gives high-level medical care at a free public hospital. The Mercy James Centre for Paediatric Surgery and Intensive Care is at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital in Blantyre. It first opened in July 2017. The singer’s non-profit group, Raising Malawi, built it with the Malawian Ministry of Health. It is still the country’s first unit made just for children’s surgery. According to updates Raising Malawi posted on its official portal and news releases on Madonna’s website, the centre has grown its work to fill a huge gap in specialist children’s healthcare in the region. More than 50 per cent of Malawi’s 20 million people are under the age of 18. Safe surgery is vital to lower the number of children who die. The centre offers free surgery for complex conditions that children are born with, serious injuries, and children’s tumors. Raising Malawi has shared recent patient stories. They include four-year-old Trevor, who had a successful corrective cardiac thoracotomy (a heart operation), and four-month-old Success, who had surgery to remove a tumor.High operating costs and infrastructure needsRunning the centre takes a lot of steady funding. Raising Malawi reports that the Mercy James Centre costs $2.4 million a year to run. The charity said on its fundraising portal that keeping up supplies of medical items, key medicines, and fuel for backup generators is a constant struggle. Changing currency values and wider economic trouble in the southern African country make it harder. To keep the centre running and widen access through regional referral networks, the charity has started a campaign to raise $12 million. Raising Malawi plans to hire more specialist staff over the next five years. This includes four paediatric surgeons, two anesthetists, four critical care nurses, two operating theatre nurses, three bio-medical engineers, and one dedicated intensivist. “The thing I’m most proud of in my life is the work I’ve done helping vulnerable children in Africa, particularly in Malawi, and of course, my incredible, beautiful children,” Madonna said during a Raising Malawi partner event in New York, as reported on her official website. “I’ve always believed that every child deserves a chance to thrive.”Professional training and national healthcare impactThe Mercy James Centre does more than perform surgeries. It is also a main training site for Malawian medical workers. The unit works with international groups. These include the children’s surgery charity KidsOR, led by co-founder Gareth Wood, and ELMA Philanthropies, headed by president Robyn Calder. Their joint aim is to train local surgeons, anaesthetists, and intensive care nurses. This builds the country’s healthcare strength over the long term. Before the centre opened, children’s surgery in Malawi was held back by serious shortages of resources. General surgeons often did complex operations on babies without special intensive care units for recovery. The Mercy James Centre has a dedicated three-bed paediatric intensive care unit. This has greatly improved survival rates after surgery. Raising Malawi confirmed that the centre also supports the surgery needs of three other central referral hospitals across the country. This means rural clinics can send young patients who need urgent surgery. Besides its main medical centre in Blantyre, Raising Malawi still pays for education and social support projects across the country. These include the Jacaranda School for Orphans, the Home of Hope Children’s Homes, and youth sports training through Ascent Soccer.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Vermont dam built around 1920 for a youth-camp pond held 24,000 cubic yards of sediment; removal opened 26 miles of stream habitat for brook trout
articles.summary: The removal of Camp Wihakowi Dam in Northfield, Vermont, has opened 26 miles of stream habitat for brook trout, restoring ecological balance and improving river safety after decades of sediment buildup. This project underscores the importance of river conservation efforts and their impact on local ecosystems and communities.
articles.body: The Camp Wihakowi Dam stood on Bull Run in Northfield, Vermont, where it had created a pond for a youth summer camp around 1920. By 2020, the breached concrete structure was responsible for accumulated sediments, restrictions on fish movement and damage to nearby land during flooding. Its removal was coordinated by Friends of the Winooski River with local landowners Lisa and Jonathan Burr and several conservation and government organisations. According to Vermont Business Magazine, the project involved a 100-foot-long dam at the former camp, which had become The Woods Lodge, an inn and retreat centre. The objective of the removal was to improve river conditions, address safety concerns and reconnect stream habitat for native fish, including brook trout.Sediment accumulation and the risks associated with the structureThe dam’s condition had implications for both the surrounding property and the river system. A partial breach during the late twentieth century had not eliminated the obstruction, and sediment continued to accumulate behind the remaining concrete. The Eastern Brook Trout Joint Venture identified the structure as a barrier to aquatic organism passage and recorded concerns about flooding, erosion, and sediment reaching the Dog River.As per the account from the Friends of the Winooski River project, Bull Run flows north from Roxbury into the Dog River at Northfield, and the watershed covers approximately 9.3 square miles, including 8.6 square miles upstream of the former dam. Before removal, the structure interfered with sediment movement through the channel, and material had accumulated upstream, while erosion affected downstream sections. Heavy rainfall, including storms following the dam’s partial breach, had been associated with flooding and damage to land and infrastructure.During a sudden breach, sediment retained behind the dam stood to move downstream and threaten river habitat. It also stood to destabilise the downstream reaches and ultimately travel towards Lake Champlain. Removing the structure therefore addressed a combination of river-management, property-safety and ecological concerns rather than fish passage alone.Engineering work restored river connectivity and floodplain accessThe removal project was initiated by Friends of the Winooski River in 2018 and commissioned MacBroom, Inc. to undertake a feasibility study and prepare the design. The permit and fundraising started in 2019, before Hilltop Construction carried out approximately twelve weeks of excavation during the summer of 2020. The financial and technical support came from the Eastern Brook Trout Joint Venture, Lake Champlain Basin Program, The Nature Conservancy, US Fish & Wildlife Service, Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, and Vermont Natural Resources Council.The planned excavation involved 24,000 cubic yards of accumulated sediment, a quantity that the project account compared with more than 1,500 full dump trucks. The impounded material had to be removed so as to restore the channel and minimise the risk of an uncontrolled sediment release.The Vermont Natural Resources Council reported that the project would reconnect 26 miles of aquatic habitat and remove the final barrier to the Dog River headwaters. Subsequently, the Eastern Brook Trout Joint Venture described the completed project as reconnecting approximately 26 miles, roughly six miles of Bull Run and 21 miles of upstream habitat, inclusive of smaller tributaries. The restoration allowed the river to regain access to its floodplain and provided space for water to spread during high flows and supported channel stability. The removal of the barrier enabled native brook trout to reach additional upstream habitat, including colder sections of the watershed that can provide refuge as summer temperatures rise.The project continued beyond the demolition and excavation work aspartners undertook further work in 2021 on the pedestrian bridge, access road and former pond area to support recovery and stabilisation. Monitoring indicated that the river was flowing freely, sediment transport had returned to more natural conditions, and vegetation was becoming established across the restored floodplain.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2012, an Australian couple bought a convict-built Georgian mansion dating to 1832 for A$500,000; after preserving its interiors for 14 years, they sold the 32-hectare estate for A$1.6 million
articles.summary: When it comes to historic homes, some are restored by changing them, while others are preserved by resisting change altogether.
articles.body: When it comes to historic homes, some are restored by changing them, while others are preserved by resisting change altogether. In Bathurst, Australia, one remarkable Georgian mansion has taken the latter path. Rainham, a heritage-listed homestead dating to 1832, has retained much of its original character through decades of careful stewardship. After more than a decade in the hands of a musician couple who deliberately left its interiors largely untouched, the sprawling estate has entered a new chapter with a A$1.6 million sale.A Georgian home with deep rootsAccording to ABC and Real Estate, Rainham sits across more than 32 hectares at 720 Vale Road, Orton Park, around five minutes from central Bathurst. The six-bedroom homestead is among the city's oldest surviving properties and was built for Captain Thomas Raine, a merchant, explorer and pastoralist.Constructed with convict labour in 1832, the property remained in the Raine family until 1854. Captain Raine lived there with his wife, Fanny, and their 10 children, and some members of the family are believed to have been buried on the estate.Rainham also has an unusual connection to one of Australia's oldest real estate brands. Captain Raine was the grandfather of Thomas Raine Jr, who later co-founded Raine & Horne, and the great-great-grandfather of Angus Raine, the company's current executive chairman.Preserving rather than renovatingAccording to records cited by ABC and Real Estate, musician Richard Miller and his flautist wife, Suzy, purchased Rainham for A$500,000 in 2012. Over their years at the property, their approach was notably different from a conventional restoration. And instead of modernising the interiors, the couple sought to preserve what remained. Original materials were retained, including ageing lino in the kitchen, while layers of wallpaper had been removed to reveal Georgian-era calcimine paint underneath. Their decision helped maintain the home's sense of authenticity, allowing future owners to encounter the property much as generations before them had.A rare sale attracts strong interestRainham had been offered for sale for more than a year before finally changing hands. Its guide price reached A$1.8 million in February, before the property ultimately sold for A$1.6 million through Raine & Horne Bathurst agent Grant Maskill-Dowton.As reported by ABC, the property generated more inquiries than any other listing the agent had marketed during the previous two years. The transaction also marked only the second time Rainham had been offered for sale in its 193-year history.The buyers are local and reportedly plan to move their Highland cattle stud to the estate while maintaining its heritage character. Rather than reworking the property wholesale, they intend to continue the conservation work started by the previous owners.A new chapter for RainhamThe sale is particularly significant given the property's connection to the Raine family. For nearly two centuries, Rainham has remained a physical link to Bathurst's early development and to the life of a pioneering family.Its latest owners now inherit more than a historic residence. They take possession of an estate whose greatest value lies in what has survived: original details, a largely untouched interior and a landscape carrying generations of history. For Rainham, the next chapter appears set to follow the same philosophy that protected its past: preserve first, improve carefully.Image Courtesy: Real EstateReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2023, a California woman paid over $40,000 for a backyard home that was never built; two brothers behind the company now face 35 felony charges each following 200 complaints in 18 counties
articles.summary: A woman in Roseville, California, who paid more than $40,000 in January 2023 to have a small home built in her backyard, was left without the house after
articles.body: A woman in Roseville, California, who paid more than $40,000 in January 2023 to have a small home built in her backyard, was left without the house after the company failed to begin construction within the promised 12 months. Three years later, brothers Austin and Colton Paulhus, founders of Anchored Tiny Homes, are facing 35 felony charges each following an investigation into more than 200 complaints across 18 California counties. Homeowners alleged that they had paid for houses that were either left unfinished or never built.Jan Truelock is a retired nurse from Roseville who had hired the company to build a 450-square-foot home behind her house, as per a report by Realtor. Such homes are known as accessory dwelling units (ADUs), which are smaller residential units built on the same property as an existing house. Truelock expected her new home to be ready in 12 months, as the company had promised. But the months went by without any construction.According to Truelock, she tried contacting the company several times to find out what was happening, but getting a response to her calls and emails became difficult. As per her account, by the time a year had passed, she had paid thousands of dollars but had nothing built in her backyard.Truelock eventually decided to cancel the agreement and asked for her money back. However, she claimed the company offered to return only $5,000 and told her that $17,000 had been spent on building materials, although she said she had never seen any of them.Truelock takes legal action With no home and no full refund, Truelock hired a lawyer and sued the company for breach of contract. She eventually reached a settlement for $25,000, which still left her short of the amount she had originally paid.She later hired another company, Imkat, to build the home. This time, the work was completed. But while Truelock finally got the additional living space she wanted, she learned that several other customers had been left in much more difficult situations.Some had paid far more than she had, while others were living with unfinished construction on their properties. Speaking to Realtor.com about the criminal case against the company's founders, Truelock said, “I’m very glad they are finally held accountable.” “Accountability at this juncture would be prison time for Colton and Austin,” she added.Families affected by the delaysOne of those customers awaiting her home was Katie Lucas, who wanted to build a separate home for her mother-in-law and grandmother in San Leandro, California.In 2022, Lucas paid Anchored Tiny Homes $211,000 for the project. Work began, but it stopped before the house was finished.Lucas told KCRA that she had made payments whenever the company sent her invoices. Later, however, contractors informed her that they had not been paid. She also said the company stopped answering her calls.When Lucas shared her experience online, she found that other homeowners were reporting similar problems. They came together in a Facebook group that, at one point, had more than 1,000 members.Another customer, Renee Kumamoto, had hoped to build a home for her father, who was battling cancer. She paid $168,000 to Anchored Tiny Homes, but construction never started.According to Kumamoto, the company went out of business just two weeks after she made her final payment.35 Felony charges against brothersAs complaints continued to emerge, California's Contractors State License Board (CSLB) began investigating the company.According to the California Statewide Law Enforcement Association (CSLEA), the board revoked Anchored Tiny Homes' contractor licence in November 2024. However, complaints continued even after the company shut down. Investigators continued examining the cases and worked with the Sacramento County District Attorney's Office to refer them for possible criminal charges.According to the criminal complaint, brothers Austin and Colton Paulhus allegedly collected more than $1 million from customers for 13 projects without carrying out the required work or supplying materials.Prosecutors also allege that more than $653,000 was taken from company accounts for expenses unrelated to construction projects.Each brother now faces 33 charges involving the alleged misuse of construction funds, one charge of conspiracy to commit a crime and one charge of employee wage theft.The brothers appeared virtually in court on October 14, but neither entered a plea. Both are also seeking bankruptcy protection in federal court. The allegations have not yet been decided by the court.The next settlement conference is scheduled for January 12. Austin Paulhus' lawyer, Blair Goss, told NBC Bay Area that his client was willing to cooperate with investigators. He declined to say whether Austin would testify against his brother.For homeowners who paid for projects that were never completed, recovering their money remains a major concern. “I have doubts that anyone else will get any of their money back,” Truelock said.You use AI every day. articles.title: American software company Palantir and London Mayor Sadiq Khan end £50 million police contract legal battle as fresh procurement process gets underway
articles.summary: Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's policing office have ended their legal dispute over a £50 million Metropolitan Police software contract, clearing
articles.body: Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's policing office have ended their legal dispute over a £50 million Metropolitan Police software contract, clearing the way for a fresh procurement process. As reported by the BBC, the settlement, announced on 15 October 2026, closes Palantir's High Court challenge but does not overturn the decision that stopped the original two-year deal. The dispute began after concerns were raised about how the Met selected a supplier and secured approval for the proposed spending. Both sides will cover their own legal costs, while Palantir remains eligible to bid again as the police force faces mounting budget pressures and potential staffing cuts.How the Palantir Metropolitan Police contract dispute beganThe dispute began in May 2026, when the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) prevented the Metropolitan Police from proceeding with a proposed two-year agreement with Palantir, the US technology company. The deal concerned software designed to help officers process intelligence and support criminal investigations, reducing the amount of manual work involved in examining information.MOPAC's objections centred on how the contract had been pursued. In correspondence with Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley, deputy mayor for policing and crime Kaya Comer-Schwartz questioned why the force had given serious consideration to only one supplier. She also said the Met had failed to obtain the necessary approval for its procurement strategy, describing the lapse as a serious breach of the rules.Palantir's legal challenge over the blocked police contractPalantir launched its High Court claim in June, disputing MOPAC's intervention. The company argued that the decision amounted to an unlawful veto and alleged that considerations about its values and ethics had been used improperly to prevent the agreement from going ahead. MOPAC rejected that account. The disagreement was heading towards a trial scheduled for January 2027. During the proceedings, searches of Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan’s text messages and emails were expected as part of the legal process, raising the prospect of closer scrutiny of communications surrounding the decision.The settlement announced on 15 October brought that prospect to an end. Neither side will pay compensation or make a payment to the other under the agreement, and each will cover its own legal expenses. The terms resolve the legal challenge without restoring the contract that the Met had originally sought.What the settlement says about Palantir's valuesA joint statement accompanying the settlement addressed the suggestion that Palantir's ethics had influenced the decision. MOPAC accepted that comments previously supplied to the media by the mayor's spokesperson might have left people with the wrong impression about the reasons for blocking the deal.The office said it was willing to correct that impression and made clear that it had no policy of refusing to contract with Palantir. It reiterated that its intervention was based on its statutory responsibilities for reviewing spending proposals and securing value for public money.Fresh procurement process puts the decision back in playMOPAC and the Metropolitan Police are now working towards running the contract process again. The joint statement said this would be done as quickly as practicable, although it did not set out a confirmed timetable for the new competition or identify which other suppliers might take part.Palantir's opportunity to bid again leaves the outcome open. The Met will still need to pursue the agreement through the renewed process, while the mayor's office retains its role in overseeing the spending decision. The settlement therefore removes the immediate legal obstacle without settling the underlying question of which supplier should provide the software.The dispute also exposed differences over how the force had approached a major technology purchase. The Met had argued that its procurement process complied with legal and commercial requirements, while MOPAC's intervention focused on the way the proposed contract had been handled. Those positions were not reconciled through a court judgment; the parties chose to settle instead.Police budget pressures remain a concernThe proposed technology deal had been presented by the Met as one way to respond to a difficult financial outlook. In June, Rowley told the London Policing Board that the Palantir system could have helped the force reduce its workforce by around 500 positions as it faced a budget shortfall of £100 million in the current year and a projected gap of £125 million in the following year.His warning placed the contract within a wider debate about how the force could manage its finances while maintaining policing services. The software was intended to support intelligence analysis, but the anticipated staffing savings also formed part of the case for pursuing the deal.Khan acknowledges Palantir's presence in LondonKhan's comments during the week of the settlement offered a further indication that the disagreement was not being presented as a blanket rejection of the company. He said Palantir contributed to employment and investment in the capital, pointing to its London workforce and the lawful use of its services by organisations in the UK and elsewhere.The statement sits alongside MOPAC's clarification that it has no standing policy against contracting with Palantir. Neither amounts to an endorsement of the original procurement process, nor does either reverse the decision that stopped the Met's proposed deal.For now, the practical outcome is limited but clear. The court challenge has ended, neither side has secured a financial payment from the other, and the £50 million contract remains subject to a new procurement exercise. Palantir can take part, but the next decision will depend on that process rather than the settlement itself.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports and official statements concerning the legal dispute between Palantir and the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime. The Times of India has not independently verified all the details.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: A family dispute over the care of a 95-year-old woman with advanced dementia in Georgia ended on Monday with a court ruling in favour of her daughter,
articles.body: A family dispute over the care of a 95-year-old woman with advanced dementia in Georgia ended on Monday with a court ruling in favour of her daughter, after her two sons challenged the decision to make her their mother's guardian.According to the case details available on Justia, the disagreement began over who should look after Janet Dixon and grew into a dispute involving restrictions on family visits, control of her money and arguments between the siblings.In its verdict, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld an earlier ruling appointing Janet's daughter, Elizabeth “Lysa” Dixon McCullough, as her guardian, finding that concerns about her brothers' conduct supported the decision.Janet has three children, including Lysa and her brothers, James “Jim” Dixon and Merritt “Sandy” Dixon. All three agreed that their mother needed someone to make decisions for her because of her condition. But while the brothers wanted Jim to remain in charge, Lysa believed she should take responsibility for their mother's care.The family had been sharing responsibility for Janet in different ways over the years. Since 2018, she had been living in a house on Jim's property. Lysa moved into the house in July 2024 and became her full-time caregiver. However, in December that year, Jim hired a professional to look after their mother instead. Lysa's relationship with the new caregiver became strained, and Jim eventually called the police on his sister.By June last year, the disagreement had reached a point where both sides wanted the court to intervene. Lysa had moved Janet to another nearby house and applied to become her guardian. Jim opposed the request and asked the court to appoint him instead. As the case progressed, the court began examining not just the siblings' disagreements but also whether Janet was being allowed to maintain contact with people close to her.Why Jim wanted guardianshipIn September 2023, before Janet was diagnosed with dementia, she had signed documents giving Jim authority to make healthcare decisions and manage her finances. She had also named Sandy as a backup healthcare agent.The court initially recognised Janet's earlier choice and appointed Jim as her temporary guardian. Janet returned to the house on his property, but the arrangement soon raised concerns about her contact with Lysa.Jim had refused to allow his sister onto the property, preventing her from visiting their mother. The court intervened and directed him to allow Lysa to see Janet and speak with her. It also warned the siblings against arguing in front of their mother, given her health condition.Meanwhile, questions were emerging about Janet's money. Jim had transferred a substantial amount of her assets into a trust. He later acknowledged moving some funds into a bank account held only in his name.Jim explained that he wanted to stop Lysa from taking the money for personal use. However, the court was concerned that some of Janet's assets had not been disclosed when Jim first sought guardianship.The court subsequently appointed county administrator Julianne Glisson to manage Janet's finances temporarily while the case continued.Mother-daughter reunion ends in disputeThe family's strained relationship became particularly clear during a meeting between Janet and Lysa, which was recorded by Janet's friend, Julie McIntosh.According to court records, Janet appeared happy to see her daughter after several weeks without contact. But the visit was interrupted when Sandy entered the room and confronted Lysa. During the encounter, Lysa fell to the floor.Sandy later claimed that Lysa had attacked him. The court did not accept his version of what happened and described the recording as horrifying. The incident became part of a wider examination of how Janet had been treated while living on Jim's property.During a three-day hearing in September 2025, some of Janet's friends told the court that Jim had restricted their telephone contact with her and discouraged them from visiting. They said Lysa had been more willing to help them stay in touch with Janet.The court also examined the handling of Janet's assets and found problems with the information the brothers had provided about her finances.Why court chose the daughter over her brothersAfter hearing evidence from the family, friends and medical professionals, the probate court decided on October 1, 2025, to appoint Lysa as Janet's permanent guardian.The judge acknowledged that Lysa had also been involved in the disagreements. However, the court described her as “not the perfect choice, only the best one available”, concluding that she could put aside the conflict with her brothers when making decisions for their mother. The court separately appointed Glisson to manage Janet's financial affairs.Jim and Sandy challenged the decision, arguing that Janet's earlier choice of Jim should have been respected and questioned the use of the recording involving Sandy and Lysa.However, the Georgia Court of Appeals found that the earlier court had sufficient reasons to choose Lysa. It pointed to concerns about Jim's conduct, the handling of Janet's assets, and the restrictions placed on her contact with others.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Floods: Building boom in Nepal and India's Uttarakhand puts 300,000 people in path of potential Himalayan disasters, study suggests
articles.summary: The construction of tourism facilities, housing, and infrastructure has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand.
articles.body:
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.

Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.

The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.

Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.

They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.

It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.

Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.

"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."

To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides .

Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."

Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."

Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.

The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".

"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."

But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants .

"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.

And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.

The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.

But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.

The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.

This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.

The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.

Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.

"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."

Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.

But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.

Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.

Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.

"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."

Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.

"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.

A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.

On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.

"You can see rampant construction all over."

The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.

But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.

Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.

But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.

articles.title: Maine girls to speak out on trans athletes as parents revive ballot push on eve of Senate election
articles.summary: Maine high school girls will speak publicly about competing against transgender athletes as nearly 5,000 new ballot initiative signatures are submitted.
articles.body: Maine high school girls will speak publicly about competing against transgender athletes Monday as parents prepare to submit nearly 5,000 additional signatures in a renewed effort to put restrictions on girls’ sports and school facilities before voters. The Nov. 2 news conference in Augusta comes one day before Maine’s closely watched Senate election, bringing renewed attention to the issue that triggered a confrontation between President Donald Trump and Democratic Gov. Janet Mills in early 2025. The Protect Girls Sports in Maine ballot committee is seeking a place on the 2027 ballot, after its earlier petition fell 532 valid signatures short of qualifying for this year’s election. Two female athletes from Windham High School and Fryeburg Academy are scheduled to participate alongside parents, representatives of Alliance Defending Freedom and the Independent Council on Women’s Sports, known as ICONS. "It’s appalling and shameful what these girls and hundreds of others have endured in Maine, and we are so glad they reached out for support," ICONS co-founder Kim Jones said in a statement ahead of the event. "Their stories are a historical dark mark on Maine’s treatment of its women and girls." FEMALE ATHLETES, WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATES SPEAK ON CAPITOL HILL AS TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE HOVERS OVER MIDTERMS "We are proud to stand alongside these young female athletes and their families to unapologetically say that women and girls deserve fair and safe sports, as well as privacy and dignity in places of undress," Jones continued. "There should be no male students on girls’ teams, and no male students in girls’ restrooms and locker rooms." The initiative, "An Act to Designate School Sports Participation and Facilities by Sex," would establish requirements based on students’ sex as recorded on their original birth certificates for participation in designated school sports and access to bathrooms and other private spaces. It would also allow students to sue schools over violations. Leyland Streiff, the ballot committee’s principal officer and a leader of Maine Girl Dads, said approximately 100 volunteers collected the additional signatures over the past month. "Despite needing only 532 more signatures to make the 2027 ballot, the committee is submitting almost 5,000," Streiff said in the event announcement. The signatures would still require review before the initiative could qualify. The renewed push follows months of litigation over the original petition. According to Maine’s Supreme Judicial Court, organizers submitted 79,692 signatures in February, and election officials initially determined that enough were valid to move the proposal forward. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS A subsequent challenge resulted in a revised determination leaving the petition below the required 67,682 valid signatures. The dispute included 1,520 signatures collected by four nonresident circulators who had not timely consented to Maine courts’ jurisdiction. The state’s highest court upheld their invalidation July 10. Organizers say they pursued a federal court challenge while collecting additional signatures to advance the initiative for 2027. Retired professional soccer player Carly Smolak, who will appear with ICONS, said the effort concerns recognition of female athletes’ accomplishments. "I am honored to stand beside these courageous soccer players to stand up for the right of every female athlete in Maine to know that her hard work, dedication and accomplishments will be honored and recognized, not overshadowed," Smolak said in the announcement. The event returns attention to a debate that put Maine at the center of national scrutiny in February 2025, when a transgender Greely High School athlete won the girls’ Class B indoor pole-vault championship. Greely won the girls’ team championship by one point. On Feb. 21, Trump confronted Mills at a White House governors’ event over Maine’s refusal to follow his executive order barring transgender athletes from female sports. Trump threatened to withhold federal funding, while Mills said she would follow state and federal law. WHERE TOP DEMOCRAT SENATE CANDIDATES AND THEIR GOP OPPONENTS STAND ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS "See you in court," Mills told him. The Maine Principals’ Association maintained that its participation policy followed the Maine Human Rights Act, which protects against discrimination based on gender identity. Mills defended her response as a stand against presidential overreach, arguing that Trump could not withhold congressionally appropriated funding to force the state to comply with his demands. Now, the renewed ballot effort coincides with a Senate contest featuring candidates with differing records on transgender participation in sports. Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson in the Nov. 3, 2026, election, a race that could help determine control of the Senate. Collins voted in March 2025 to advance the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act. Explaining her support for a similar amendment in March 2026, she said her longstanding position was that "transgender athletes should not compete in girls’ and women’s athletics." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Jackson voted in June 2023 to accept a committee recommendation against passing LD 930, legislation seeking to restrict participation in women’s and girls’ scholastic sports. In an April 2026 questionnaire during his gubernatorial campaign, he also answered "No" to a question asking whether he supported a transgender sports ban and dismantling other protections under the Maine Human Rights Act. Jones said advocates intend to continue pressing the issue through elections and other avenues. "The feelings of boys do not take precedence in the areas and opportunities set aside to let girls thrive," she said. "An ever-growing wave of public support exists to ensure that girls in blue states have a light at the end of the tunnel." "The men who want to protect their daughters, the young female athletes, and the public are not going to let up," Jones continued. "The courts, the voting booth, the media and every other available tool will be used to ensure that these girls are not shoved into the shadows to be harassed and ignored." articles.title: Dia de Finados: veja o que abre e o que fecha no Grande Recife | G1
articles.standfirst: Feriado nacional, que cai na segunda-feira (2), altera funcionamento de serviços. Ponto facultativo para servidores públicos foi transferido da quarta (28) para sexta-feira (30).
articles.summary: Feriado nacional, que cai na segunda-feira (2), altera funcionamento de serviços. Ponto facultativo para servidores públicos foi transferido da quarta (28) para sexta-feira (30).
articles.body:
Cemitério de Santo Amaro, na área central do Recife — Foto: Hélia Scheppa/Divulgação

Celebrado na segunda-feira (2), o feriado de Finados altera o funcionamento do comércio, de repartições públicas e de espaços culturais. Também haverá uma programação religiosa com missas no Recife , de acordo com a prefeitura ( veja mais abaixo ).

Além disso, a data vai emendar com o Dia do Servidor Público, que caiu na quarta-feira (28), mas o ponto facultativo foi transferido para a sexta (30), tanto no governo do estado quanto na prefeitura do Recife. Assim, os trabalhadores terão um feriado mais prolongado, somando quatro dias de descanso.

Confira, abaixo, como ficam os serviços e a programação religiosa durante o feriado de Finados:

A maioria dos shoppings do Grande Recife funciona em horário especial:

Na segunda-feira (2), não haverá expediente nas agências dos Correios. As unidades funcionarão normalmente na sexta-feira (30) e retornam às atividades no dia útil seguinte ao feriado, a terça-feira (3). Aquelas que operam aos sábados abrirão como de costume.

Os endereços e horários das agências podem ser consultados na internet . Durante o feriado, a Central de Atendimento estará disponível somente por meio de canais automatizados:

Autoatendimento pelos telefones 0800-725-7282, 0800-725-0100 e 3003-0100.

O atendimento automatizado funciona 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana.

As agências bancárias também não abrem. A Federação Brasileira de Bancos (Febraban) orienta os clientes a utilizarem preferencialmente os canais digitais, como sites e aplicativo dos bancos, para a realização de transferências e pagamento de contas.

As compensações bancárias, incluindo a TED, não são efetivadas nos feriados. Somente o PIX funciona normalmente.

A Febraban orienta, ainda, que os boletos de cobrança e contas de consumo (água, energia, telefone, entre outros) com vencimento no feriado poderão ser pagos, sem acréscimo, no dia útil seguinte. Já o pagamento dos tributos e impostos, caso vençam nos dias em que não há compensação bancária, deve ser antecipado.

Os espaços culturais do Recife terão funcionamento especial durante o feriadão do Dia do Servidor e Finados. Museus e teatros municipais não abrem ao público às segundas-feiras, com exceção dos espaços que têm programação específica.

O Paço do Frevo e a Casa do Carnaval terão atividades especiais. Já o Parque das Esculturas e o Jardim Botânico funcionarão em horários diferenciados. Confira os horários:

Domingo (1º): Arrastão do Frevo, com concentração a partir das 15h30, na Praça do Arsenal. O cortejo contará com mais de 30 blocos líricos.

De sexta-feira (30) a segunda-feira (2): programação do 18º Seminário do Ciclo Junino, com atividades voltadas à cultura popular e aos concursos de quadrilhas juninas.

Sexta-feira (30) e segunda-feira (2): fechado.

Sábado (31) e domingo (1º): funcionamento normal.

Sexta-feira (30), sábado (31) e domingo (1º): funcionamento normal.

Os demais museus e teatros municipais estarão fechados na sexta-feira e na segunda. Durante o fim de semana, sábado (31) e domingo (1º), o funcionamento normal. A única exceção será o Museu de Arte Moderno Aloísio Magalhães (Mamam), que está sem exposições em cartaz no momento e ficará fechado de sexta a segunda.

Os parques urbanos administrados pela Autarquia de Manutenção e Limpeza Urbana do Recife (Emlurb) funcionarão normalmente durante o feriadão de Finados. Confira os horários:

A Ciclofaixa de Turismo e Lazer do Recife estará montada no domingo (1º) e na segunda-feira (2), das 7h às 16h. O Corredor Recife de Esporte e Lazer também funcionará normalmente no sábado (31), das 4h às 7h30.

Entre a sexta (30) e a segunda (2), os mercados públicos e as feiras livres do Recife funcionam das 6h às 18h, com exceção do domingo, quando o horário é reduzido, das 6h às 13h. As praças de alimentação podem estender o atendimento após as 18h.

Para atendimentos de urgência, emergência e internação, o funcionamento segue 24 horas nas seguintes unidades de saúde:

Policlínica Agamenon Magalhães (Afogados)

Policlínica Amaury Coutinho (Campina do Barreto);

Policlínica e maternidade Professor Barros Lima (Casa Amarela);

Policlínica e maternidade Professor Arnaldo Marques (Ibura);

Maternidade Professor Bandeira Filho (Afogados);

Hospital pediátrico Helena Moura (Tamarineira);

Os Centros de Vacinação estarão funcionando com a oferta de multivacinação e Influenza para todos os públicos. Na sexta (30) e no sábado (31), o funcionamento será das 9h às 19h nos shoppings Boa Vista, Riomar e Recife. No domingo (1°) e na segunda (2), será das 11h às 19h no Shopping Boa Vista e das 12h às 19h no Recife e no RioMar.

Já o Hospital Veterinário do Recife funciona normalmente durante o feriado, com atendimento 24 horas para casos de urgência e emergência. Os serviços ambulatoriais retornam à normalidade a partir de terça-feira (3).

As unidades da Academia da Cidade funcionam normalmente na sexta (30) e no sábado, das 8h às 12h, fechando no domingo e na segunda.

Em relação à vigilância ambiental, o Centro de Vigilância Ambiental e Controle de Zoonoses do Recife (CVA) realiza plantão para atendimento de emergências envolvendo animais que ofereçam risco à saúde pública. O serviço pode ser acionado das 8h às 17h, por meio mensagens ou ligações para o Whatsapp (81) 3355-7712.

Na segunda-feira (2), no Cemitério de Santo Amaro, na área central do Recife, estão previstas quatro missas. São elas:

às 7h, presidida pelo padre João Crisóstomo;

às 10h, com o arcebispo metropolitano de Olinda e Recife, Dom Paulo Jackson;

ao meio-dia, com o bispo auxiliar Dom Josivaldo Bezerra;

No Cemitério Parque das Flores, no bairro do Curado, na Zona Sul do Recife, a programação terá início às 7h. Confira o cronograma:

às 9h, com padre Gilson, vigário episcopal de Jardim São Paulo;

às 11h, com Dom Josivaldo Bezerra, bispo auxiliar de Olinda e Recife;

às 14h, com monsenhor Luciano Brito, vigário-geral da Arquidiocese de Olinda e Recife;

às 16h, presidida por Dom Fernando Saburido, arcebispo emérito de Olinda e Recife.

No Cemitério de Casa Amarela, na Zona Norte do Recife, a programação organizada pela Paróquia Santa Isabel Rainha de Portugal prevê três missas, às 9h, 11h e 15h.

Já no Cemitério da Várzea, na Zona Oeste da cidade, está prevista uma celebração às 9h, organizada pela Paróquia Nossa Senhora do Rosário.
