articles.title: Quando é o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026? Veja data | G1
articles.standfirst: Confira quando cai o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026 e a data limite para o pagamento do salário.
articles.summary: Confira quando cai o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026 e a data limite para o pagamento do salário.
articles.body:
Confira quando cai o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026 e a data limite para o pagamento do salário. — Foto: Rafa Neddermeyer/Agência Brasil

Para trabalhadores com carteira assinada, o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026 será sexta-feira, dia 6 . Para o cálculo do prazo de pagamento de salários, o sábado é considerado dia útil, enquanto domingos e feriados não entram na contagem.

A regra está prevista no artigo 459 da Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT), que determina que o salário deve ser pago, no máximo, até o quinto dia útil do mês seguinte ao trabalhado.

Quando é o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026?

No cálculo do prazo para pagamento do salário, são considerados os dias de segunda-feira a sábado. Domingos e feriados ficam fora da contagem.

Primeiro dia útil: 2 de novembro (segunda-feira);

Segundo dia útil: 3 de novembro (terça-feira);

Terceiro dia útil: 4 de novembro (quarta-feira);

Quarto dia útil: 5 de novembro (quinta-feira);

Quinto dia útil: 6 de novembro (sexta-feira).

Portanto, para quem trabalha com carteira assinada, o quinto dia útil de novembro de 2026 é a sexta-feira (6).

Sábado conta como dia útil para o pagamento do salário?

Sim. Para a contagem do prazo previsto na CLT para o pagamento de salários, o sábado é considerado dia útil.

A contagem é interrompida aos domingos e feriados. Por isso, mesmo que o trabalhador não tenha expediente aos sábados, o dia entra no cálculo do quinto dia útil.

Essa regra é específica para o prazo de pagamento do salário e não significa que o sábado seja necessariamente um dia normal de trabalho para todos os empregados.

O que acontece se o salário não for pago até o quinto dia útil?

O artigo 459 da CLT estabelece o prazo máximo para o pagamento do salário. Se o empregador não cumprir a data-limite, o trabalhador pode buscar orientação para cobrar os valores atrasados.

Em caso de atraso, o empregado pode recorrer à Justiça do Trabalho para cobrar o pagamento devido, com os acréscimos que forem aplicáveis. O sindicato da categoria também pode auxiliar na defesa dos direitos dos trabalhadores e na adoção das medidas cabíveis.

Atrasos frequentes ou prolongados no pagamento podem caracterizar descumprimento das obrigações do empregador.

Dependendo das circunstâncias e da gravidade da situação, isso pode levar ao reconhecimento da rescisão indireta, quando o trabalhador encerra o contrato por falta grave do empregador e pode ter direito às verbas de uma demissão sem justa causa.

O empregador também pode estar sujeito à fiscalização e às penalidades previstas na legislação trabalhista.

articles.title: 'I live with a ghost': Japan's haunted homes attract bargain hunters
articles.summary: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.
articles.body:
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.

"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.

"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."

While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.

"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.

Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.

Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.

For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state. For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."

The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.

But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

'If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her'

The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.

Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.

"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.

It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.

Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap.

Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

articles.title: No clear winner in Israel election with nearly 90 percent of votes counted
articles.summary: Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc leads but is falling short of the votes needed to form a government.
articles.body:
No clear winner has emerged from Israel’s election , with nearly 90 percent of ballots counted and both major political blocs falling short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The Israeli Central Elections Committee said on Wednesday that it had counted more than five million votes as of 9pm local time (19:00 GMT). Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is on course to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is expected to secure 48 seats.

Projections from Tuesday’s voting also showed that the Arab parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – could hold a record combined 19 seats.

Final election results could come as early as Thursday evening, though no clear winner is expected to emerge.

More than 500,000 special double-envelope ballots remain to be counted, potentially changing the seat distribution. These include votes cast by soldiers, diplomats and others voting away from their registered polling stations.

The vote – the first since the October 7, 2023, attacks and the Gaza genocide – was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s premiership. The 77-year-old appears far from defeated, despite lacking a clear majority.

Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. President Isaac Herzog will begin consulting party leaders about forming a new administration next week, once the official election results are released.

Herzog has urged all parties to avoid another vote that would stall the formation of a government. But coalition building is the norm in Israel, and no party has ever won an outright majority in the country’s history.

Ahead of the vote, Eisenkot ruled out forming a minority government with Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has also rejected such a prospect.

As Netanyahu’s bloc is set to be the largest, analysts predict that he will form a unity government that could include Eisenkot. However, such an outcome is far from certain.

Eisenkot said in a post on X on Wednesday that his opposition alliance was now focused on the “heavy task entrusted to us – bringing change to Israel and establishing a Zionist mobilisation government”.

“This is the will of the people who expressed no confidence in the government of October 7th and the shirking, and in the bloc of shirkers in general. A bloc that is at the low point of two decades.”

Amid record turnout among Arab voters, Netanyahu’s Likud party accused Arab parties of stealing the election.

“The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilise voters,” the party said in a statement.

“The Likud party is transferring to the police, the Shin Bet, and the Central Elections Committee hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence regarding election theft in many Arab polling stations,” it said.

Israel’s predominantly Arab Joint List political alliance said in a statement published late on Wednesday by Turkish news agency Anadolu that preliminary figures showed Arab voter turnout played a decisive role in keeping Netanyahu and his coalition short of a parliamentary majority, while cautioning that the final results were yet to be announced.

Voters answered incitement and intimidation at the ballot box, it said, rejecting a “government of butchers” and its policies of home demolitions, racism and war crimes.

The Joint List said its electoral support reflected demands for political unity and a force capable of defending Arab citizens’ rights without concessions.

It pledged to work to remove Netanyahu’s government and prevent its return, saying it was ready to cooperate towards an alternative government.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said the alliance could back an anti-Netanyahu government from outside, but would not join it.

articles.title: George Michael: Family row over dozens items up for auction
articles.summary: The brother of the singer's late personal assistant says she would not have wanted the items to be sold.
articles.body:
A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.

The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.

Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.

Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.

Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.

Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.

There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.

Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".

He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".

Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.

Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

It has an estimated price tag of between £60,000 and £120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.

A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to £600 and a current bid of £1,750.

Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

articles.title: Weight-loss jab boom brings Coventry needles warning for recyclers
articles.summary: Recycling bosses say used needles are increasingly being found among household waste.
articles.body:
The boom in injectable weight-loss drugs , such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, is leading to more used needles turning up at recycling centres, putting workers at risk of serious injury and infection, bosses say.

At a recycling plant in Coventry, I watched staff sorting rubbish on a fast-moving conveyor belt when a crushed yellow sharps container suddenly appeared among the waste.

"A resident has put this in a wheelie bin," explained supervisor Paul Pagett.

"It then gets crushed by the recycling vehicle and then it comes to us open and obviously we've got needles then falling out onto the line putting my guys at risk."

The sharps box should never have been there.

Used needles should be disposed of separately through dedicated clinical waste services. Instead, recycling bosses say they are increasingly finding them mixed in with household waste.

"There are safe disposal routes for needles but the worst place to put them is in your recycling," said Richard Dobbs, managing director of Sherborne Recycling.

"It ends up in facilities like ours where it will be touched by people and that's inherently unsafe."

Sherborne Recycling handles waste from several local authorities and serves about 1.5 million residents.

The plant is highly automated, but workers still have to remove items that cannot be processed and regularly inspect waste to check what is being sent for recycling.

That means employees can potentially come into direct contact with discarded needles.

Paul Pagett showed me a cupboard stacked with yellow sharps containers that have all been recovered from the recycling stream since the start of the year.

Some are likely to have come from people using medicines such as insulin, where patients are often given sharps bins and advice on disposal.

But recycling bosses say the growing popularity of privately prescribed weight-loss injections has created a new challenge.

Many people buy the drugs privately and may not automatically receive a sharps box or guidance on how to dispose of used needles safely.

The result is that large numbers are ending up in household bins and, in some cases, recycling collections.

For workers, the consequences can be serious.

Dobbs described what happens when someone accidentally sticks themselves with a used needle.

"It's a worrying time. You have to be tested and wait for results. It can take months," he said.

"Most of the time they're clear but on occasion there will be times when people have picked up serious infections and illnesses and that's obviously devastating for them."

At Sherborne, only a handful of staff come into direct contact with waste.

In other recycling plants, dozens of workers might be exposed.

The advice is simple: Speak to your GP or pharmacy about obtaining a sharps bin and how to dispose of it safely.

Whatever you do, never put a sharps container or loose needles in your recycling bin.

articles.title: Strikes on Darfur market in Sudan killed more than 100, rights group says
articles.summary: Women and children killed as witnesses say attack struck civilian shopkeepers, RSF fighters.
articles.body:
Military drone strikes in southwestern Sudan’s Darfur that killed more than 100 people – mostly women and children – earlier this week targeted a busy city market frequented by paramilitary fighters, witnesses said.

Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence, put the toll from Monday’s attacks at more than 100 dead and 113 wounded.

While Emergency Lawyers reported that most of the victims were women and children, witnesses said on Wednesday that multiple civilian vendors who sold goods to paramilitary fighters were among those killed in the attack in Nyala, the South Darfur city that serves as the de facto capital of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The war between the RSF and the army, now in its fourth year, has created severe poverty, food shortages and the world’s worst displacement crisis.

A cigarette vendor told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that hundreds of RSF fighters gathered at the market on the evening of the attack. He said that he moved his stall between gatherings of the paramilitary fighters to sell cigarettes and that a drone struck around 8pm (18:00 GMT), killing dozens of fighters and women selling food.

Another witness told the AP that the explosion was massive and killed many fighters. He estimated that around 14 civilians, including women and children, were also killed, most of them women selling tea and food.

Both spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation.

Mubarak Bekheit, an aid worker in Darfur, said on Wednesday that many people remained missing and some bodies had yet to be recovered from homes in the area after the strike hit a civilian neighbourhood.

“I personally know that war has no morality, but the reality we witness every day is that civilians are the ones paying the highest price. They lose their lives, their loved ones, and their homes, while living under the constant fear of further bombardment,” he said.

Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces fighting with the army, wrote on Facebook that more than “150 militia recruits” were killed at the Dumaya camp, west of Nyala, in what he described as a “precise and targeted air strike”.

Casualty figures from Monday’s attack are unconfirmed and could not be independently verified amid limited information from the city. Sudan Doctors Network, another group that tracks violence, issued a statement on Wednesday preliminarily reporting 21 dead and more than 40 wounded, saying shelling caused most of the deaths.

“The release of this statement was delayed … given the challenges of accessing field documentation sources within Nyala amid ongoing active military operations and security constraints that hinder efforts to monitor and verify the conditions of victims and the injured,” the group said.

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said that a second strike hit a civilian neighbourhood after the market attack. MSF said a hospital it supports in Nyala received 36 bodies in the hours after the strike, 21 of them wearing civilian clothing, and that its teams saw more than 150 wounded in the emergency room.

“Markets, homes, and key civilian infrastructure are not targets,” the group said in a statement. “All parties to the conflict must protect civilians.”

Drone strikes have become the leading cause of civilian deaths in Sudan, the United Nations reported, in a war that has pushed parts of the country into famine . In RSF-controlled Nyala, the share of children seeking treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from 5 to 11 percent, according to UN estimates released earlier this month.

articles.title: When a well struck oil on his Pennsylvania farm in 1865, John Benninghoff leased plots to drillers; one account put the farmer’s monthly income at an unverified $40,000
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of John Benninghoff, a Pennsylvania farmer who struck oil in the 1860s and generated an astonishing income of $40,000 per month, revolutionizing the oil industry and leading to a frenzied drilling boom.
articles.body: The oil-producing area in northwestern Pennsylvania in the 1860s consisted of a series of farms. Landowners on the hills overlooking the creeks suddenly found themselves at the center of a drilling colony if they had even one productive well. Since land ownership provided individual access to the surface and minerals below it, operators usually had to obtain the land either via lease or purchase. The payments on lease could be made in cash or as a proportion of the oil extracted or both. Many holders subdivided their land to allow drilling from several operators at once. Income from such subdivisions was reported in newspapers, but it was not always accurate. The case of a farmer near Oil Creek demonstrates how far off some numbers could be.A farmer, born in 1801, whose land lay on a tributary of Oil CreekJohn Benninghoff was born on December 25, 1801, in Lehigh County, Pennsylvania, a date and place given by both the Erie Reader and the Mercer County PAGenWeb biography, which reproduces the 1888 History of Mercer County. Around 1831, the family moved from Clearfield County to Venango County, where he rented farmland for several years before buying his own and in April 1868 he sold his lands and moved to Greenville in Mercer County. His farm lay along Benninghoff Run, a tributary of Oil Creek, as the Erie Reader and the Early Oil Pipelines history at petroleumhistory.org both describe it.Sources disagree on the size of his farm. The Erie Reader describes a 57-acre farm, the Mercer County PAGenWeb biography drawn from the 1888 History of Mercer County gives 235 acres and a Benninghoff family history on Pennsylvania Genealogy gives 300 acres. The same county history dates his oil interest from 1861 to April 1868.The Ocean Well and disputed production figuresThe Ocean Well, drilled on the slope of a hill in fall 1865, is cited by the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources as a departure from the prevailing view that drilling needed flat land. Once the well began producing 300 barrels a day, operators rushed to lease parts of the farm and Benninghoff soon earned about $6,000 a day, the department reports. John J. McLaurin’s Sketches in Crude Oil gives an initial flow of 600 barrels per day from September 1, 1865, but the Pennsylvania Geological Survey puts the flow of the Ocean well, completed in 1865 along Benninghoff Run, at 300 barrels per day. The park’s Benninghoff Farm Tableau has six derricks, each 35 feet high, along with an oil barge and an engine house, as the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources describes it.Benninghoff City and Henry Harley’s two-mile pipeline route in late 1865A settlement took its name from the Benninghoff farm. In late 1865, Henry Harley, a commission dealer, began laying two two-inch pipelines from Benninghoff City to his tanks at the Shaffer railroad yard, a distance of two miles, as the Early Oil Pipelines history at petroleumhistory.org describes.The pipelines threatened the livelihood of the teamsters who hauled oil by wagon and in late 1865 angry teamsters set fire to Harley’s wooden tanks at Shaffer. Incendiary fires were also set at several other sites, including Benninghoff Run, where deaths resulted.Income estimates of $50,000 a month and $6,000 a dayThe Erie Reader puts the family income at $50,000 per month. The Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources puts his earnings at about $6,000 a day, which would total $180,000 over 30 days at that pace. Neither figure is a verified account. Wells on Benninghoff’s land produced between 25 and 300 barrels of oil per day, as recorded in John J. McLaurin’s Sketches in Crude Oil.The January 16, 1868 robbery and conflicting accounts of the sum stolenAccounts of the robbery differ on the sum stolen. The History of Mercer County, reproduced by the Mercer County PAGenWeb biography, puts it at $250,000, the Erie Reader gives $260,000 and McLaurin’s Sketches in Crude Oil gives $265,000. The county history adds that none of the money was recovered and that the family spent $50,000 trying to capture the robbers, whereas the Erie Reader says the reward grew to $50,000. The same history records that Benninghoff sold his lands in April 1868, moved to Greenville and died worth around $400,000.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russia says more than 600 drones launched towards Moscow overnight
articles.summary: The attack is the latest in a series of major drone assaults targeting the Moscow region.
articles.body:
Russia has downed most of the 613 drones launched towards Moscow overnight, in a major attack on the Russian capital, Russian state news agency TASS has reported.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that air defence forces destroyed 231 of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on approach to the city, with the remainder neutralised on distant approaches between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.

articles.title: In 2017, a 41-year-old Michigan mother died following cosmetic surgery and five days in hospital; an appeals court has upheld a $9.7 million verdict finding the hospital negligent
articles.summary: A Michigan appeals court has upheld a nearly $9.7 million judgment against Henry Ford Macomb Hospital in the case of a 41-year-old mother of two who died
articles.body: A Michigan appeals court has upheld a nearly $9.7 million judgment against Henry Ford Macomb Hospital in the case of a 41-year-old mother of two who died after developing a severe infection following cosmetic surgery in 2017. In a ruling dated October 23, 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals rejected the hospital’s challenges to the verdict, finding no errors that warranted overturning the judgment.The case centres on the death of Cathleen Allen, who underwent an abdominoplasty, commonly known as a tummy tuck, on May 26, 2017. According to the court’s opinion, Allen was admitted to Henry Ford Macomb Hospital’s emergency department on June 2 with chills, pain, weakness, fatigue, confusion and an inability to eat. She was treated in the intensive care unit (ICU) for five days before suffering cardiac arrest and being pronounced dead.The lawsuit alleged that delays in treating an infection following the operation contributed to Allen’s death. While the jury found the surgeon professionally negligent, it separately held the hospital administratively negligent for failing to ensure that its patient-safety procedures were properly implemented and enforced.Disagreement over infection delayed treatmentAccording to the appellate ruling, doctors suspected that Allen was suffering from septic shock when she arrived at the hospital. Her attending physician in the ICU, Ghada Mesleh, believed the shock was caused by an infection originating in the abdominal wound from her recent surgery. Mesleh consulted Vijay K. Dixit, the plastic surgeon who had performed Allen’s tummy tuck. However, Dixit initially advised doctors to look for another source of infection and did not believe that surgical intervention was necessary at that stage. The disagreement continued over the following days as ICU doctors evaluated possible sources of the infection. The court record states that Dixit eventually operated on Allen on June 6, the day she died.The estate’s case argued that the delay in addressing the suspected abdominal infection prevented timely treatment. Medical experts who testified at trial said that controlling the source of an infection is critical when treating septic shock and that earlier intervention could have changed the outcome.James Attarian, an expert in internal medicine and hospital administration, testified that if doctors had surgically treated the infection during the first few days of Allen’s hospital admission, she would have survived, according to the court opinion. His assessment was part of the evidence presented to the jury rather than a separate finding by the appeals court.Why the hospital was held administratively negligentA central issue in the case was whether Henry Ford Macomb Hospital had implemented and enforced its internal “chain of command” policy. Such procedures are designed to help medical staff escalate concerns when disagreements over patient care remain unresolved and could put a patient at risk. The plaintiff argued that the hospital failed to ensure the policy was understood and followed, allowing the disagreement over Allen’s treatment to persist without an effective escalation process.During the trial, the hospital’s former chief of surgery, Harold Gallick, testified that he was initially unfamiliar with the concept of a chain of command in healthcare. He also said he did not believe a written policy specifically covered a situation in which doctors held opposing views that could affect a patient’s treatment.The court record further noted that several witnesses had limited familiarity with the hospital’s policy when they were first questioned. The policy’s delayed disclosure also led to witnesses being deposed a second time.Experts for Allen’s estate argued that a hospital must do more than establish safety procedures on paper: it must make sure staff members know how to use them and that they are enforced when necessary. They said the unresolved disagreement over Allen’s infection was precisely the kind of situation in which escalation should have occurred.The hospital disputed the allegations. Its defence included testimony that staff members could obtain second opinions and had authority to seek additional medical assistance. A defence expert also argued that the hospital had taken reasonable steps to implement its procedures.After an 11-day trial in 2023, the jury found Dixit professionally negligent and Henry Ford Macomb Hospital administratively negligent. It determined that both forms of negligence were proximate causes of Allen’s death. The hospital’s liability was based on its own administrative failures, rather than simply being held responsible for the surgeon’s conduct.Appeals court rejects hospital’s challengesThe hospital appealed the judgment, contesting aspects of the damages award, the jury instructions and the handling of discovery related to its internal policies. In its October 23 ruling, the Michigan Court of Appeals rejected the arguments it considered and affirmed the judgment. The court concluded that the evidence supported the jury’s finding that failures involving the hospital’s policies and patient-safety obligations contributed to the delay in Allen’s treatment.The judgment included $4,336,988 for Allen’s future lost earning capacity, alongside other economic and non-economic damages. The hospital argued that the lost-earning-capacity award was not recoverable in the form presented under Michigan’s wrongful-death law. The appeals court, however, found that the estate had also pursued damages for the loss of financial support suffered by Allen’s children and that the record supported the award.The ruling also addressed the hospital’s objections to the jury instructions concerning statutory duties to provide adequate and appropriate care. The court found no basis to reverse the judgment on those grounds. The surgeon and Cosmetic and Plastic Surgery Clinic were not parties to this latest appeal. The opinion notes that a satisfaction of judgment had been entered in relation to those defendants.Allen’s death left behind two children, who were 19 and 15 at the time, according to the court record. The estate argued that her death caused not only personal loss but also the loss of financial support she had provided to them.The case highlights the role hospital administration can play in patient safety, particularly when doctors disagree over diagnosis or treatment. The appellate ruling underscores that patient-safety policies must be effective in practice, not merely exist on paper, when delays in care may have serious consequences.You use AI every day.
